title: Clearfield Trust Co. v. United States (1943)
summary: Federal law governed the rights arising from the United States’ disbursement check, and delayed notice did not defeat recovery without a showing of resulting prejudice.
notes:
The surrounding Parnell and Kimbell Foods notes qualify automatic assumptions of federal uniformity. A federal connection does not mean every private dispute requires a newly created federal rule.

Justice Douglas wrote for the Court; a 1936 WPA check payable to Clair Barner was stolen, forged and cashed at a J. C. Penney store in Clearfield, Pennsylvania, the district court applied Pennsylvania law and ruled for the bank on the government's delay, the Third Circuit reversed, and the Supreme Court affirmed, holding that the rights and duties of the United States on its own commercial paper are governed by federal law fashioned by the federal courts, since applying varying state rules would create uncertainty for a nationwide program.

sections.Parties: The United States sought recovery on a check bearing a forged endorsement from the financial institution that had guaranteed prior endorsements.
sections.Material Facts: A federal disbursement check was stolen or wrongfully endorsed and passed through a retailer and banking channels. The government delayed notifying the collecting institution of the forgery. The institution invoked that delay to resist reimbursement. The transaction involved the United States’ own payment obligations, rather than only a private commercial dispute involving a federal document.
sections.Procedural History: The Supreme Court applied federal law and rejected an automatic bar based solely on delayed notification.
sections.Issue: What law governed the United States’ rights on its payment instrument, and did delay alone defeat its claim?
sections.Holding: Federal law governed. The party relying on the delay had to show the relevant prejudice; it was not presumed merely from the passage of time.
sections.Reasoning: The government’s issuance of checks arose from federal functions, and a uniform rule could avoid having those obligations vary with the geographic route of a check. The Court therefore identified a specialized federal lawmaking interest despite Erie’s rejection of federal general common law. The case also shows that selecting federal law and specifying its content are separate tasks. The content here protected the government’s claim unless the institution established a loss attributable to the delay.

learning.why: Federal law governed the rights arising from the United States’ disbursement check, and delayed notice did not defeat recovery without a showing of resulting prejudice.

topics.cp-federal-common-law: Federal payment instruments implicated a federal interest supporting a federal rule.
topics.cp-federalism: The Court considered whether borrowing varying state rules would impair uniform federal operations.
topics.cp-erie: Clearfield is the standard illustration that Erie does not govern where a federal interest calls for federal common law.
topics.cp-usc-1652: The opinion treats the Rules of Decision Act as inapplicable to the government's own commercial paper because federal, not state, law supplies the rule.
